preamble: The voiced retroflex stop [ɖ] can lenite to a rhotic when the closure weakens into a trill and the place shifts forward. The clearest case is Romani, which rhoticized Middle Indo-Aryan retroflex stops (ḍ, ṭ, ḍḍ, ṭṭ, ḍh) to a second rhotic ř, phonetically a uvular [ʀ] or long trill [rː] in conservative dialects; in the many dialects that merged ř with r, the outcome is plain /r/. Thus Prakrit ḍoṃba, the name of a caste of travelling musicians, became Romani rrom 'Romani man', and *maṇḍa became manřo 'bread'. Other Indo-Aryan languages instead keep the retroflex place, giving an intervocalic flap [ɽ].

examples.from: Prakrit ḍoṃba (Sanskrit ḍomba) 'member of a caste of travelling musicians'
examples.note: Dialects continue the retroflex differently: ř [ʀ, rː] in conservative varieties, plain r where ř merged with r, and l elsewhere (lom).
The retroflex stop after the nasal became ř; other dialects have mando or manlo.
